key_terms.meaning: Implanted or external device that gives a small timed current pulse to start a heartbeat when natural conduction fails.
Device that gives one large controlled shock to stop chaotic fibrillation so a normal rhythm can restart.
Cardiopulmonary bypass circuit that pumps blood and oxygenates it while the heart is stopped.
The rule that ends each breath: set volume, set pressure, set time, set flow or the patient's own effort.
Device that adds water vapour to dry medical gas before it reaches the airway.
Device that turns liquid medicine or water into fine droplets for inhalation.
Deep heating by radio-frequency current, commonly 27.12 MHz, passed through tissue without cutting skin.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation; low-amplitude pulses through skin used mainly to relieve pain.
Neuromuscular electrical stimulation; current pulses that make a muscle contract for training or function.
Electrical muscle stimulation; use of current pulses to produce muscle contraction.
Functional electrical stimulation; NMES timed to help a useful movement such as grasping or walking.
Two medium-frequency currents crossed in tissue; their difference frequency stimulates nerve.
Time for which each current pulse is on, usually measured in microseconds or milliseconds.
Number of pulses or cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Strength of a current or voltage pulse, measured in milliamperes (mA) or volts (V).
Q = I × t, where I is current in amperes and t is pulse width in seconds; measured in coulombs (C).
Breaking a kidney stone with focused shock waves so small pieces pass out in urine.
Cold probe cooled by liquid nitrogen or expanding gas that freezes and destroys tissue.
Circuit that limits the high shock voltage reaching an ECG amplifier during defibrillation.
Catheter that delivers radio-frequency energy to destroy a small patch of heart muscle causing an arrhythmia.

takeaways: A pacemaker gives a small timed pulse to start a beat; a defibrillator gives one large shock to stop fibrillation.
A heart-lung machine replaces both the heart's pumping and the lung's gas exchange during open-heart surgery.
A ventilator mode is named by the variable that ends each breath: volume, pressure, time, flow or the patient.
Dry medical gas injures the airway, so water is added as vapour, droplets or a measured inhaled drug dose.
Diathermy heats deep tissue with radio-frequency current, microwaves or ultrasound without cutting the skin.
Electrical stimulation uses controlled current pulses to relieve pain, retrain muscle or find a nerve.
Lithotripsy breaks stones with focused shock waves, and cryotherapy destroys lesions with deep cold.
Protection circuits and careful catheter energy delivery keep therapeutic shocks from damaging the patient or the monitor.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for block diagrams, waveforms, electrode or catheter placement, mode selection, safety hazards, and internal-versus-external comparisons.

glossary.def: A device that gives a small timed electrical pulse to the heart when natural conduction fails.
A device that delivers a large controlled shock to stop ventricular fibrillation.
A heart-lung machine circuit that pumps and oxygenates blood while the heart is stopped.
A machine that moves a breath into the lungs and lets it out.
A device that adds water vapour to dry medical gas.
A device that turns liquid into fine droplets for inhalation.
A device that delivers a measured drug dose to the airway.
Deep heating of tissue by radio-frequency current, microwaves or ultrasound.
Diathermy using radio-frequency current, commonly 27.12 MHz.
Diathermy using microwave energy, commonly 2.45 GHz.
Deep heating by high-frequency sound waves passed into tissue.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, used mainly for pain relief.
Neuromuscular electrical stimulation, used to make muscles contract.
Electrical muscle stimulation, a general term for current pulses that cause muscle contraction.
Functional electrical stimulation, NMES timed to help a useful movement.
A short interrupted current used to stimulate nerve and muscle.
A steady direct current used in some electrotherapy treatments.
A medium-frequency alternating current used for muscle strengthening.
Two crossed medium-frequency currents that produce a low difference frequency in tissue.
Breaking a kidney stone with focused shock waves.
Destruction of tissue by local freezing below about −40 °C.
A circuit that protects an ECG amplifier from a defibrillator shock.
A catheter that delivers radio-frequency energy to destroy an arrhythmia-causing patch of heart muscle.
The on-time of one electrical pulse.
Current multiplied by pulse width, Q = I × t, in coulombs.
